WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As he walks past the tiny, dingy waiting area into an equally cramped garage, Nui Srisook says business at his car repair shop is thriving. Drivers are choosing to keep their old cars longer, and they're turning to repair shops to make it so, observers say. Sales are up 20 percent this month and Srisook spends most nights working late, helping his customers to get extra mileage out of their old cars. "Most of the customers right now we see, they don't really have much extra money to ... buy a new car. So that's why they just do repair," Srisook said. "And now, people are willing to spend more money on maintaining the car, deciding what is broke, anything that needs to be maintained on the car." As more cash-strapped Americans turn to do-it-yourself projects and bargain shopping, car repair shops like Srisook's are feeling the boon. Drivers are choosing to keep their old cars longer, and often they're willing to put in the money to do so, observers say. The Automotive Service Association reports their members' sales were up 16 percent over last year.  Watch Kate Bolduan's report on the thriving auto repair industry » . "That indicated that people were coming in and putting the vehicle in the repair facilities' hands and saying, 'Look, I am going to be keeping this car. I want to be sure it runs well. I want to be sure that if there are any safety issues or any maintenance issues that I have overlooked, let's get those taken care of,' " said ASA President Ron Pyle. Pyle said that's a change from the past, when drivers would scrimp on the cost of maintenance and repair. "That was surprising news. We didn't expect that in the midst of the beginnings of the economic woes," Pyle said. "But they are looking at the cost of trying to purchase a new vehicle ... so I think that in relative terms that $1,000 repair to keep a $2,500 car running may be an attractive alternative." The economic slump has cut automakers deeply. Last month, sales of new cars were down more than 40 percent compared with the same time last year, according to sales tracker Autodata. The trend seems to have translated into increased traffic at auto parts stores. "We're doing way more business. The phones are ringing, you know, customers are walking in," said Darryl Wright, owner of D.C. Brake & Bearings Co. "Basically, if it's broke, they fix it." In the past, only savvy auto mechanics knew to shop at Wright's nondescript discount store. Now, he sees more car owners who are looking for a cheaper deal on parts. "[Customers will] find a guy on the street, you know -- Joe Shady Mechanics is what we call them -- to fix it at a deeper discount rate, labor-wise, and they'll send the customer in here to buy the parts on their own," Wright said. "So people are saving money that way too." Srisook said he keeps service prices low to appeal to those bargain shoppers, such as Esther White, a loyal customer. She brought in her daughter's 1996 Oldsmobile for new rotors and brakes, and said her daughter would be driving the car "until it drops dead." "Believe it or not, we were raised to fix things, and to hold on to things as long as we could," White said. "But it goes back to today's economy, and making the right financial decisions."

# Auto Repair Industry Thrives Amid Economic Downturn

While many businesses struggle during difficult economic times, car repair shops across the country are experiencing an unexpected surge in demand. Nui Srisook's repair shop exemplifies this trend, with sales climbing 20 percent this month as customers increasingly invest in maintaining their existing vehicles rather than replacing them.

This boom reflects a broader shift in consumer behavior. Cash-strapped Americans are choosing to hold onto their older cars longer instead of purchasing new ones, driving a significant increase in demand for repair and maintenance services. As household budgets tighten, keeping a current vehicle running has become a practical financial decision for many drivers.

The trend extends well beyond individual shops. According to the Automotive Service Association, its members reported sales up 16 percent over the previous year—a surprising development given the broader economic troubles affecting so many other industries. This growth highlights how the repair sector has become a rare bright spot in an otherwise challenging economy.

Perhaps most notable is the change in how drivers approach vehicle maintenance. In the past, many would scrimp on repair costs, deferring service whenever possible. Today, however, drivers are far more willing to spend money on proactive maintenance and essential safety repairs, recognizing the long-term value of keeping their vehicles in good condition.

The economics behind this shift are compelling. For many consumers, investing in repairs has become an attractive alternative to buying new. Spending $1,000 to keep a $2,500 car running reliably is considerably more affordable than taking on the expense of a new vehicle during an economic slump. As a result, repair shops like Srisook's continue to see steady business, proving that hard times can create opportunity in unexpected places.

# The Rise of Auto Repair in a Cost-Conscious Economy

Amid ongoing economic hardship, a notable shift is taking place in how Americans approach car ownership. Faced with tight budgets, rising costs, and uncertainty about the future, many drivers are choosing to hold onto their older vehicles and invest in repairs rather than commit to the significant expense of purchasing a new car. For countless households, the math is simple: maintaining a paid-off vehicle is far less costly than taking on a new auto loan and the accompanying monthly payments, insurance increases, and depreciation.

This change in consumer behavior has driven more people through the doors of auto repair shops across the country. Where car owners once might have replaced an aging vehicle at the first sign of trouble, they are now opting for maintenance and upkeep to extend the life of the cars they already own. Routine services, part replacements, and mechanical fixes have become a practical alternative to buying new, allowing drivers to stretch their dollars further while keeping their vehicles reliably on the road.

The benefits of this trend have been felt strongly within the auto repair industry. The Automotive Service Association reported a 16 percent increase in sales over the previous year—a substantial jump that reflects the growing demand for repair services. For an industry that has traditionally competed against the appeal of shiny new models on dealership lots, this surge represents a welcome and significant boost.

Perhaps most striking is how this signals a departure from long-standing consumer habits. In more prosperous times, drivers typically sought to minimize their repair spending, viewing maintenance as an unwelcome cost to be avoided or delayed whenever possible. Today, however, that mindset has reversed. Repairs are increasingly seen not as a burden but as a smart financial decision—a way to preserve value and avoid larger expenses down the line. As economic pressures persist, this pragmatic approach to vehicle ownership appears poised to remain a defining feature of the American automotive landscape.

# Economic Uncertainty Keeps Americans Behind the Wheel of Aging Cars, Boosting Repair Business

*By CNN Business Staff*

As economic pressures squeeze household budgets across the country, Americans are increasingly choosing to repair their aging vehicles rather than purchase new ones—creating a boom for auto repair shops and parts retailers nationwide.

The average age of vehicles on U.S. roads has climbed to a record high, with many drivers deciding that maintaining their current cars makes more financial sense than taking on new auto loans amid elevated interest rates and rising sticker prices.

## Repair Shops See Surge in Business

For independent repair shops, the trend has meant a noticeable uptick in customers seeking to extend the life of their vehicles.

"We've never been busier," said Maria Gonzalez, owner of Gonzalez Auto Care in suburban Chicago. "People are coming in wanting to fix things they might have ignored a few years ago. They're investing in their current cars because a new one just isn't in the budget right now. We're seeing a lot of repairs that keep these vehicles running for another 50,000 or even 100,000 miles."

Gonzalez said her shop has expanded its hours and is considering hiring an additional technician to keep up with demand.

## Parts Retailers Benefit Too

The ripple effect extends to auto parts stores, where owners report increased sales as more consumers—and do-it-yourself mechanics—stock up on components.

"Our sales are up significantly compared to last year," said Rick Thompson, who owns an independent auto parts store in Dallas. "We're seeing everything from brake pads to alternators flying off the shelves. A lot of folks are learning to do minor repairs themselves to save on labor costs. When money's tight, people get resourceful."

## Industry Leaders Weigh In

Industry observers say the shift reflects broader economic anxieties, but they note that keeping older vehicles well-maintained can be a smart financial move.

"When consumers feel uncertain about the economy, one of the first things they do is postpone big-ticket purchases like a new car," said James Whitfield, president of the National Automotive Service Alliance. "That directly benefits the repair and maintenance sector. We're seeing sustained growth, and we expect this trend to continue as long as new vehicle prices and financing costs remain high. The average car today is built to last much longer than it was decades ago, which makes repairing them a viable option."

## Customers Making the Practical Choice

For everyday drivers, the decision often comes down to simple math.

"I've had my car for twelve years now, and honestly, it still runs great after some work," said Denise Carter, a customer at Gonzalez's shop who recently paid for a new transmission. "I looked at what a new car would cost me every month, and it just didn't make sense. Spending a couple thousand on repairs is a lot cheaper than a $600 monthly payment. I'm going to keep this car running as long as I can."

Carter's sentiment echoes across the industry, where repair shop waiting rooms are increasingly full of customers making similar calculations.

## Looking Ahead

Analysts suggest the trend could persist well into the coming year, particularly if economic conditions remain challenging. While the automotive sales sector may feel the strain, the aftermarket repair and parts industries appear poised to continue thriving.

For business owners like Gonzalez, the shift represents an unexpected silver lining in uncertain times.

"When the economy is tough, people take care of what they have," she said. "And right now, that's keeping our doors open and our bays full."

---

*This article is a fictional sample created for illustrative purposes.*

# Independent Auto Shops See Uptick as Drivers Keep Aging Cars on the Road

*Economic downturn drives customers away from dealerships and new car lots toward local repair businesses*

As families across the country tighten their budgets amid economic uncertainty, an unexpected group is finding reason for optimism: independent auto repair shop owners.

With new car prices remaining high and many consumers reluctant to take on additional debt, more drivers are choosing to maintain and repair their existing vehicles rather than purchase replacements. That shift is translating into steady, and in some cases growing, business for small repair shops.

"People are holding onto their cars longer than they used to," said Marcus Delgado, who has owned a three-bay repair shop in a Midwestern suburb for the past 14 years. "A few years ago, someone with a car problem might just trade it in. Now they're calling us to fix it and keep it running another year or two."

## A Countercyclical Business

Auto repair has long been considered somewhat resilient during economic downturns. When money is tight, industry analysts note, consumers defer large purchases like new vehicles but still need reliable transportation to get to work and manage daily life. That makes ongoing maintenance a necessity rather than a luxury.

"The average age of vehicles on the road has been climbing for years, and downturns tend to accelerate that trend," said one industry observer. "Every additional year a car stays in service is more potential work for the local mechanic."

For small business owners, that dynamic can provide a measure of stability that other industries lack.

## Local Shops Gaining Ground

Some independent operators say they are also winning customers who previously relied on dealership service departments, where labor rates and parts costs are often higher.

"We're seeing folks who used to only go to the dealer," said Rita Chen, who runs a family-owned shop with her husband. "They're comparing prices now more than ever, and we can usually save them money on the same repair."

Chen said her shop has added weekend hours to accommodate demand and recently hired an additional technician—a rare instance of hiring during a period when many businesses are cutting back.

## Challenges Remain

The picture is not entirely rosy. Shop owners point to rising costs for parts and equipment, supply chain delays for certain components, and difficulty finding qualified technicians as ongoing pressures on their bottom line.

"Business coming in the door is good, but our expenses are up too," Delgado noted. "And skilled mechanics are hard to find. If I could hire two good techs tomorrow, I would."

There is also the reality that customers stretched thin financially sometimes delay recommended repairs, occasionally leading to bigger problems—and bigger bills—down the road.

## Looking Ahead

Still, for many small business owners in the sector, the current environment offers a rare bright spot.

"You never want to root for hard times," Chen said. "But when people need to make what they have last longer, that's exactly what we help them do. In a way, our whole business is about getting more life out of something people already own."

As economic conditions continue to shape consumer behavior, independent repair shops appear positioned to keep their lifts busy—one aging sedan at a time.

# As New Car Costs Soar, Americans Turn Wrench on the Family Sedan

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — With sticker shock keeping many Americans out of dealership showrooms, a growing number of cash-strapped drivers are rolling up their sleeves and keeping their aging vehicles running the old-fashioned way: fixing them themselves.

Auto industry analysts say the shift reflects a broader economic anxiety gripping households squeezed by inflation, high interest rates and stagnant wages. Rather than take on a new monthly car payment averaging more than $730, many consumers are choosing to nurse older models past the 150,000-mile mark.

"People are doing the math, and the math says keep the car you have," said Marcus Delgado, an automotive market analyst based in the capital. "When financing a new vehicle can add hundreds of dollars to your monthly budget, a $400 repair suddenly looks like a bargain."

## Sales Slump at the Showroom

New vehicle sales have felt the pinch. Industry figures show new car and light truck sales down roughly 8 percent compared with the same period last year, as buyers balk at prices that have climbed nearly 25 percent over the past four years.

The average age of vehicles on American roads has climbed to a record 12.6 years, according to industry tracking data — a figure that has risen steadily as owners hold onto cars longer than ever before.

"We're seeing customers who would normally trade in every three or four years now stretching to seven, eight, even ten," said one suburban Virginia dealership manager who asked not to be named. "The trade-in just isn't happening the way it used to."

## Boom Times for Parts and Repairs

The flip side of the slump has been a windfall for the auto parts and repair sector. Major aftermarket parts retailers have reported quarterly sales gains in the high single digits, with do-it-yourself categories leading the growth.

Independent repair shops report similar momentum. A national trade group representing service centers estimated that repair-order volume is up about 11 percent year-over-year, with demand especially strong for brakes, batteries, timing belts and other maintenance work on higher-mileage vehicles.

"Our phones don't stop," said Angela Ruiz, who owns a three-bay garage in Maryland. "People want to keep what they've got running, and they're asking a lot more questions about what they can do themselves versus what they need us for."

## The Rise of the Weekend Mechanic

For many, YouTube tutorials and online forums have become the modern-day shop manual. Searches for repair how-to videos have surged, and parts sellers say they are stocking more entry-level tools and diagnostic scanners aimed at first-time home mechanics.

Tom Bickford, a 43-year-old federal contractor from Alexandria, said he replaced the alternator on his 2013 sedan last month after watching a 20-minute video.

"The shop quoted me almost $600," Bickford said. "The part cost me $140 online, and I spent a Saturday afternoon on it. That's a no-brainer when money's tight."

Bargain hunting has extended to salvage yards and online marketplaces, where used and refurbished components sell at steep discounts. Some drivers say they now cross-shop parts the way they once shopped for the cars themselves.

## A Trend With Staying Power

Analysts caution that the do-it-yourself surge carries risks — botched repairs can compound costs, and not every job is suited for a driveway. But few expect the broader trend to reverse soon.

"As long as new cars stay this expensive and household budgets stay this tight, the used vehicle on the road today is the vehicle people are going to fight to keep," Delgado said. "The repair economy is the new car economy, at least for now."

For drivers like Bickford, the calculation is simple.

"A new car is a dream right now," he said, wiping grease from his hands. "This? This is reality. And honestly, it's kind of satisfying."

# Making It Last: How One Mechanic's Shop Reflects a Nation Holding On to Its Cars

At 7:30 on a Tuesday morning, the roll-up door at Nui's Auto Care is already open, and the waiting room chairs are already filling. By the time Nui Srisook finishes her first cup of coffee, three vehicles are up on lifts, and two more sit in the gravel lot waiting their turn.

"Ten years ago, this parking lot was half empty most mornings," Srisook says, wiping her hands on a shop rag. "Now people are booking a week out. And it's not because I got famous. It's because nobody wants to buy a new car right now."

## A Shop Built on Trust

Srisook opened her shop twelve years ago after nearly two decades working under other people's names in dealership service departments. She started with two bays and a reputation for straight talk—telling customers what needed fixing now, what could wait, and, occasionally, what didn't need fixing at all.

"People remember when you tell them *not* to spend money," she laughs. "That's how you build a customer for twenty years instead of one visit."

That philosophy has served her well, but she's the first to admit the current boom has less to do with her charm and more to do with math.

## The Economics of Holding On

The numbers tell a clear story. The average price of a new vehicle has climbed to levels that put a fresh purchase out of reach for many working families, while higher interest rates have pushed monthly loan payments to eye-watering heights. Used car prices, too, spiked and have remained stubbornly elevated.

Faced with a choice between a hefty new car payment and a repair bill, more drivers are choosing the repair.

"A customer came in last month with a fifteen-year-old sedan," Srisook recalls. "Needed a new water pump, some belts, a brake job—about eleven hundred dollars all told. She almost cried, thinking it was too much. I told her, 'That's two car payments. This car has years left in it.' She kept the car."

The average age of vehicles on the road has reached a record high, and mechanics like Srisook are on the front lines of that trend. Cars that once would have been traded in at the first major repair are now being nursed toward the 200,000-mile mark and beyond.

## Busier, But Not Simpler

The surge in business hasn't been without challenges. Older vehicles require more labor-intensive work, and sourcing parts for discontinued models can send Srisook and her three employees on hunts through salvage yards and specialty suppliers.

"An older car is more honest to work on, but it's also more work," she says. "Rust, worn-out bolts, parts they stopped making. Sometimes I spend more time finding the part than installing it."

She's also had to invest in diagnostic equipment to service the increasingly computerized vehicles from the 2010s that are now aging into her wheelhouse. "People think old cars are all wrenches and grease. Now even a 'basic' car has a dozen computers in it."

To keep up with demand, Srisook has hired a fourth technician and is considering adding two more bays—an expansion she never imagined making a few years ago.

## A Changing Relationship With the Car

Beyond the economics, Srisook senses a shift in how her customers think about their vehicles. Where a car was once something to be upgraded every few years, many now see it as an asset to be maintained.

"I have young customers coming in asking how to make their car last," she says. "They want a maintenance schedule. They want to learn. That didn't used to happen. People are treating cars like they treat their phones now—they want to keep them running longer instead of replacing them."

She's started offering what she calls "longevity checkups"—comprehensive inspections aimed at helping owners plan repairs before something breaks on the highway.

## Looking Ahead

Srisook is realistic about the future. If new car prices and interest rates ease, she knows some of her customers will eventually trade up. But she doesn't expect the fundamental shift to reverse entirely.

"People got a taste of what it's like to keep a car going and not have that payment hanging over them," she says. "Some of them are never going back."

For now, the phone keeps ringing, the lifts keep rising, and the gravel lot keeps filling. Srisook glances at the schedule board, already crowded with names.

"I used to worry about where the next customer was coming from," she says. "Now I worry about where I'm going to put them all."

She smiles, and heads back toward the bays.

"Good problem to have."

---

*Nui's Auto Care is open Monday through Saturday. Appointments are recommended—and, these days, essential.*

# As Wallets Tighten, Americans Keep Their Cars Running Longer—and Repair Shops Are Booming

*Auto parts retailers and independent mechanics report surging demand as consumers delay big purchases and squeeze more miles from aging vehicles*

---

When Maria Delgado's 2013 Honda Accord started making a grinding noise last month, her first instinct wasn't to browse dealership lots for a shiny replacement. Instead, the 44-year-old nurse from Columbus, Ohio, drove straight to her neighborhood repair shop.

"A new car payment right now? No way," Delgado said, waiting in the lobby as a technician replaced her brake pads and rotors. "I paid off this car three years ago. I'd rather put a few hundred dollars into it and keep driving than take on a $500-a-month loan."

Delgado is part of a growing wave of American consumers who, facing economic uncertainty and elevated prices for new vehicles, are choosing to maintain and repair what they already own. The shift is proving to be a windfall for the auto repair and parts industries, which are reporting notable gains even as other sectors of the economy show signs of consumer belt-tightening.

## A Countercyclical Winner

The automotive aftermarket—the industry encompassing replacement parts, accessories, and repair services—has long been considered relatively recession-resistant. When money gets tight, the logic goes, people fix rather than replace.

"We tend to do well when consumers feel financially pressured," said Bill Hanvey, president and CEO of the Auto Care Association, an industry trade group. "The average age of vehicles on American roads has climbed past 12.5 years, an all-time high. Every one of those aging vehicles needs parts, maintenance, and repairs. When people hold onto cars longer, that translates directly into business for our members."

Industry data supports the trend. Major auto parts retailers have posted steady same-store sales growth, with executives frequently citing the aging vehicle fleet and cost-conscious consumers as tailwinds during recent earnings calls.

## Independent Shops Feel the Surge

For independent mechanics, the increase in business is tangible.

"We're booked out two weeks, sometimes three," said Tony Ramirez, who owns a five-bay repair shop outside Phoenix. "A couple years ago, if a customer had a $2,000 repair on an older car, half of them would just decide to trade it in. Now they're saying, 'Fix it. I'm keeping it.'"

Ramirez said he's seen a particular uptick in what he calls "deferred maintenance catching up"—timing belts, suspension work, and transmission service on vehicles with well over 100,000 miles.

"People are more willing to invest in the big repairs because the alternative—a new car—feels out of reach," he said.

## The Math Behind the Trend

The economics driving consumer behavior are straightforward. With new vehicle prices remaining elevated and auto loan interest rates significantly higher than they were a few years ago, monthly payments on a new car can easily exceed several hundred dollars.

By contrast, even a substantial repair often costs less than a few months of car payments.

"It's a rational calculation," said Dr. Emily Chen, an economist specializing in consumer behavior. "When financing costs are high and household budgets are stretched, the marginal cost of keeping an existing vehicle looks very attractive compared to the sticker shock of buying new. We're seeing consumers extend the life of durable goods across the board, but cars are the most visible example because they're such a large expense."

Chen noted that the trend also reflects broader anxiety about the economy. "Even consumers who could technically afford a new car are hesitant to commit to long-term debt when they're uncertain about their job security or future income."

## DIY Repairs on the Rise

The pinch is also driving more consumers to attempt repairs themselves, boosting the retail parts side of the business.

At a national auto parts chain in suburban Atlanta, store manager Devon Whitaker says he's noticed more first-time DIY customers.

"We get a lot of folks coming in who've watched a YouTube video and want to try changing their own brakes or replacing a battery," Whitaker said. "We'll loan out tools, look up the part, walk them through it. People are trying to save on labor costs any way they can."

James Okafor, a 29-year-old graphic designer, recently replaced his own alternator after getting a quote from a shop.

"The part was about $150. The shop wanted to charge me another couple hundred for labor," Okafor said. "I spent an afternoon on it with some online tutorials. It was frustrating, but I saved real money."

## Challenges Amid the Boom

The increased demand isn't without complications. Some shop owners report difficulty finding qualified technicians to keep up with the workload, reflecting a persistent labor shortage in the skilled trades.

"The business is there, but finding good mechanics is the hard part," Ramirez said. "I could use two more techs right now."

Supply chain issues that plagued the industry in recent years have largely eased, but some specialty parts still see delays, occasionally leaving customers waiting longer for repairs.

## Looking Ahead

Industry observers expect the trend to continue as long as economic conditions keep consumers cautious.

"As long as new car affordability remains a challenge and people feel uncertain, the aftermarket will benefit," Hanvey said. "Cars don't stop needing maintenance. If anything, older cars need more of it."

For consumers like Delgado, the decision comes down to practicality.

"My mechanic told me this car has another hundred thousand miles in it if I take care of it," she said, keys in hand as she headed back to her freshly repaired Accord. "That works for me. I'll keep coming back here before I ever step foot on a car lot."

---

*Reporting reflects broad industry trends. Individual customer and shop owner accounts are illustrative of patterns described by industry sources.*
